endorsements.quote: Simultaneously, reactive methods like incident reporting and peer review help identify and mitigate risks once they materialize, enabling a swift response and a process analysis to prevent recurrence.

endorsements.quote: In addition, we advocate for the implementation of formal procedures for reporting and investigating adverse events, near misses, and other safety-related incidents linked to the use of AI in healthcare settings.

endorsements.quote: We recommend mandatory incident reporting systems for translation-related adverse events, periodic comprehension audits using standardised protocols, patient feedback mechanisms to flag translation problems directly and defined trigger metrics that would prompt revalidation when error rates exceed specified thresholds.

endorsements.quote: Operationally, this requires three commitments: (1) prospective, real-world evaluations in GP; (2) equity-stratified performance reporting guided by frameworks, such as PROGRESS-Plus; and (3) rigorous postmarket surveillance with drift and subgroup monitoring and WHO International Classification for Patient Safety–aligned incident reporting.

endorsements.quote: And harm reporting asks whether standardised AI incident-reporting infrastructure is being built in primary care, equivalent to the systems that already exist for medication errors and adverse events.

endorsements.title: Mental Health Innovation Is Scaling Faster Than Accountability
endorsements.quote: Higher-risk tools delivering regulated treatment, autonomous monitoring, diagnostic support or clinician-supervised interventions should require independent evidence, defined accountability, adverse-event and near-miss reporting, performance-drift monitoring, periodic audit and explicit harm-remediation obligations.

evidence.title: Lessons Learned and Iterative Enhancements: A 2-Year Experience with an Established Responsible AI Framework
evidence.outcome: AI-involvement flags in existing patient safety event reporting
evidence.effect: Flagging mechanism captured 13 low severity AI-related events over six months
evidence.quote: To support post-evaluation monitoring, existing patient safety infrastructure was expanded by incorporating mechanisms to flag potential involvement of AI tools in reported events, resulting in only 13 low severity events over six months.

commentary.bottom_line: One uncontrolled US deployment study found that adding AI-involvement flags to an existing patient safety event reporting system captured 13 low severity AI-related events over six months. The study had no comparison period or group, so it cannot show whether flags raise detection or improve classification, and support for standard definitions and minimum report fields rests on endorsing frameworks and commentaries.

perspectives.view: The single test (epmc:PPR1258899) uses a pre-post design without a comparator and covers 64 evaluations of 55 AI solutions in a US deployment. It reports counts of flagged events but no baseline capture rate and no test of standard definitions or minimum fields. Risk of bias, indirectness, and imprecision lower certainty to very low.

All 13 events captured in six months were low severity. This suggests the flag can surface minor AI concerns, but the study does not show whether serious harms are reported, whether near misses are recognized as AI-related, or whether reports led to fixes before patients were affected. The share of AI incidents that went unreported was not measured.

The study added a flag to an existing reporting system rather than building a new one, which matches the CHAI and RUAIH advice to use current structures. The available findings do not describe reporter burden, how staff judged AI involvement, or agreement between reviewers on classification, so the fidelity of flagging in routine workflow is unknown.

The study shows that an AI-involvement flag was added to an existing reporting system in a deployment covering 55 AI solutions. It does not report staffing, review time, or cost, so administrators cannot yet estimate the resources needed to triage and analyze AI-flagged reports or to add the structured prompts that CHAI recommends.

NIST AI 600-1 ties generative AI incident reporting to existing legal duties such as HIPAA breach reporting. No study examined whether AI tags in internal systems help organizations meet external reporting obligations or align with device adverse event reporting, so the regulatory value of the practice is untested.

commentary.research_gap: Studies should compare AI-tagged reporting against a baseline period or an independent detection method such as chart review or trigger tools to estimate capture rates. They should also test whether standard definitions and minimum report fields produce consistent classification across reviewers, whether higher-severity events and near misses are reported, what staff time the process requires, and whether tagged reports lead to corrective actions.
commentary.underserved_note: The one test did not report whether its setting or reported events involved Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. Because harms in these groups, such as the AI translation errors raised in one commentary, may be less visible to the clinicians who file reports, the study gives no assurance that tagging captures incidents affecting these patients.
